reasons.detail: R1 — Implementation now always attempts `git worktree remove <path>` first in `removeWorktreeForCleanup`, and only branches to force logic on submodule-specific failure.
R2 — On submodule-related removal failure, it calls `inspectSubmoduleWorktreeCleanliness`, which runs porcelain status on the worktree root and each initialized submodule before forcing removal.

R3 — If cleanliness is confirmed (root and submodules clean), code performs one `git worktree remove --force <path>` retry and returns success only when that retry succeeds, allowing subsequent branch delete/teardown flow.

R4 — When dirty root or initialized submodule state is detected, it returns `SUBMODULE_WORKTREE_DIRTY`, includes bounded `dirtyRootFiles`/`dirtySubmodules`, and exits before branch deletion (retaining worktree and feature branch).
R5 — Non-submodule failures now return the existing `WORKTREE_REMOVE_FAILED` envelope/message, matching prior behavior and guidance.

R6 — Successful path still runs through existing teardown sequence after worktree removal (including report handling, last-finalized write, active-flow clear, branch delete, and validation calls) with only the remove strategy changed.
R7 — Status-inspection failures now return `SUBMODULE_WORKTREE_STATUS_FAILED` with bounded status failure details and recovery options, while keeping worktree/branch by returning early.
R8 — Clean-confirmed force removal failure now returns `SUBMODULE_WORKTREE_FORCE_REMOVE_FAILED`, preserves worktree and branch, and aborts before branch deletion by early return.
R9 — Dirty/status-failed/force-failed diagnostics are bounded via entry/text limits and include captured git stdout/stderr details, so errors are surfaced rather than discarded.
